analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to vote every federal regulation into law before it can take effect.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee on March 12, 1997, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, federal agencies write and issue most detailed rules — on clean air, workplace safety, food and drugs, banking — and those rules take effect without Congress voting on them. This bill would end that: no regulation could take effect until both the House and Senate pass a bill containing its exact text, and the President signs it. It sets a fast-track process with no committee review, limited debate, and a required vote within 60 days. Supporters said this forces elected lawmakers to own every rule; in practice, with thousands of rules issued each year, most would never get a vote and would simply die.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses and industries regulated by federal agencies. Any rule they oppose could be blocked or stalled by a single chamber, and most rules would likely never reach a vote at all, since Congress handles only a few hundred bills a year while agencies issue thousands of rules. Members of Congress also gain a tool to kill unpopular rules without having to legislate replacements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries and their members of Congress

how_it_helps.text: No federal regulation could take effect until Congress passes a bill made up solely of that regulation's text, so businesses could not be bound by any rule Congress never approved.

The bill includes fast-track procedures — no committee referral, debate capped at one hour, amendments banned, and a final vote required within 60 calendar days — designed to keep Congress from simply ignoring new rules.
Rules enacted through this process would no longer count as agency action for court review, moving legal challenges from agencies to the elected Congress.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on federal rules — clean air and water standards, workplace and mine safety, food and drug safety, auto safety, consumer financial protections. Most of these rules would never get floor time in a Congress that handles a few hundred bills a year, so the practical effect would be that few new protections ever take effect, even when Congress has already ordered an agency in law to write them.

drawbacks.text: Agencies issue thousands of regulations each year to carry out laws Congress has already passed; requiring a separate enacted bill for each one means most rules would die for lack of floor time, leaving laws on the books that agencies could not enforce in detail.

Even with the bill's 60-day fast track, one chamber could effectively kill any rule by refusing to act, giving a narrow bloc of legislators a veto over health, safety, and environmental protections without a recorded vote.

A fair objection supporters would raise: agencies are unelected, and Congress routinely delegates lawmaking to them and then avoids responsibility for the results — this bill tries to answer a real accountability problem, but the cost would fall on the public protections built through that process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability argument is genuine: Congress does write broad laws and lets unelected agency staff fill in the binding details, and this bill would force a recorded vote on every rule. But the design does not scale. Requiring full enactment of thousands of rules a year would not make Congress more accountable in any practical sense — it would mostly mean that new rules never take effect, which is why the bill functions as a deregulation measure that would benefit regulated industries at the expense of the protections ordinary people get from those rules. A better-designed accountability tool might target major rules or require up-or-down votes on high-impact ones rather than every rule.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Sam Brownback introduced the Congressional Responsibility Act of 1997 on March 12, 1997, joined by six original cosponsors including Sens. Kyl, Allard, Coats, Enzi, Hagel, and Sessions.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Governmental Affairs the same day; that was the last recorded action of any kind.

The bill would have barred any regulation from taking effect until Congress enacted a bill consisting solely of that regulation's text, with fast-track floor procedures and a required vote within 60 calendar days.
Twelve Republican senators cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The bill received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no further action of any kind through the end of the 105th Congress on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies kept their authority to issue rules without a separate act of Congress, and the existing body of health, safety, environmental, and consumer regulations continued to operate as before. Businesses subject to regulation were spared nothing, because nothing changed — but the members and interests hoping to use congressional gridlock as a filter against new rules also never got that tool, and the public never lost the rule-based protections it relies on.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies and the public protections they enforce

for.name: Sen. Sam Brownback
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 12 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all recorded cosponsors were Republicans.

against.name: Sen. Fred Thompson
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Governmental Affairs
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred to his committee; the bill sat without action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so there is no roll-call record; the only measurable support was partisan — all 13 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the committee chairman who let the bill die was also a Republican.

industries.note: If enacted, the bill would have given any regulated industry a practical veto over new rules, since a single chamber could decline to act and most rules would never reach a vote. The gain for industry would come at the direct cost of health, safety, and environmental protections for the public.

Agencies would lose their core power to make binding rules; every rule would need an act of Congress to take effect. Because agencies carry out protections the public depends on, their interest in keeping that power ran alongside the public's.
